extracted.intended_audience: general readers, film students, scholars and practitioners interested in silent-era comedy and Buster Keaton's techniques
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting evaluative criteria and stylistic standards illustrated by Buster Keaton's career and films—i.e., what makes effective silent/physical comedy according to the article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deadpan / stoic facial delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequently maintained a stoic, deadpan facial expression that became his trademark and earned him the nickname "The Great Stone Face."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of a neutral/stony expression to contrast with physical mayhem; reduces visible performer laughter (Keaton adopted deadpan because his laughing reduced audience laughter). Example: Keaton adopted the deadpan to regain laughs in his vaudeville act. Anti-pattern: performers who visibly laugh while doing a stunt can lessen the gag's impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical comedy and inventive stunts
rubrics_metrics.description: Performed physical comedy and inventive stunts in silent films during the 1920s; many memorable sequences depended on novel physical ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize inventive, image-driven stunt concepts and physical gags (e.g., water-tower sequence in Sherlock Jr., facade falling in Steamboat Bill, Jr.). Originality of the stunt/gag is central to comedic payoff. Examples in the article show stunts as the core of Keaton's comic identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision and technical execution of stunts
rubrics_metrics.description: Dangerous stunts required precision: Keaton described landing techniques and sequences often depended on exact positioning (e.g., standing on a mark so a building facade would pass safely).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-precision rehearsal and execution are required both for performer safety and to achieve the intended visual joke. Keaton: "The secret is in landing limp and breaking the fall with a foot or a hand." Anti-pattern: sloppy timing/placement ruins the gag and endangers performers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity of comic premises and storytelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Keaton: 'the best comedies are simple.' He removed many superfluous characters and subplots from scripts to keep comedy focused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor simple premises, fewer characters, and streamlined plots so visual gags can breathe. Examples: Keaton edited scripts down (took out '40 useless characters') to preserve clarity and pace. Anti-pattern: overcomplicated plots that dilute gag density.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pantomime and visual storytelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Keaton's work often employed long stretches of pantomime; visual action and pantomime were central to communication and comedy in silent film.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use clear pantomime and visual beats to convey motivations and jokes without spoken dialogue. In silent-era contexts, extended pantomime sequences can be effective; ensure gestures and staging read clearly to the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gag invention and authorship
rubrics_metrics.description: The most ingenious gags were generally conceived by Keaton himself; he was noted for thinking up his best gags rather than borrowing them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize original gag-creation and personal authorship of comic set pieces. Anti-pattern: relying primarily on others' recycled jokes will yield weaker, less distinctive comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of parody and burlesque
rubrics_metrics.description: Keaton experimented with parody, often targeting melodramas and established cinematic plots, structures and devices (e.g., The Frozen North satirizing William S. Hart's Western melodramas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parody succeeds when audiences recognize the target; use mimicry of genre conventions, intertitles, costume, and situational inversion to produce comedic commentary. Anti-pattern: parody so obscure or mean-spirited that the target isn't recognized or alienates the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale and use of location / scenic staging
rubrics_metrics.description: Keaton employed picturesque locations and large-scale physical set pieces (e.g., the locomotive chase in The General) to combine spectacle with comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use real locations and large-scale props to create epic visual gags and increase production scope when appropriate. Guidance: such staging can raise comedic stakes but demands logistical planning and can be expensive; ensure the gag justifies the scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of dramatic tone and comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Some Keaton films (e.g., The General) blended dramatic material with comedy and were criticized for being 'too dramatic' for audiences expecting lightweight fare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully balance seriousness and comedy—leaning too far into drama can reduce immediate laugh frequency or confuse audience expectations. Test tone against intended audience expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recycling vaudeville material judiciously
rubrics_metrics.description: Keaton sometimes recycled ideas from his family vaudeville act and earlier films in later shorts and Educational Pictures two-reelers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reusing proven bits is acceptable if they are restaged or adapted creatively for the medium; avoid mere repetition without renewal. Examples: Educational two-reelers recycled earlier gags but with new staging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creative control and independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Keaton's loss of artistic independence at MGM coincided with a decline in the quality of his work; studio interference (overplanning, production managers, forced scripts) limited his ability to stage gags his way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain as much creative control as feasible over gag staging and pace; heavy-handed production processes that over-script and bureaucratize comedy development can reduce the effectiveness of visual gags. Anti-pattern: treating comedy like a factory process with excessive approvals and restrictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performer-authenticity vs. safety trade-offs
rubrics_metrics.description: Keaton insisted on doing his own dangerous stunts ('Stuntmen don't get you laughs'), but studios sometimes insisted on stunt doubles to protect investments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh authenticity (performer doing the stunt) against safety and insurance concerns; authenticity can heighten comedic impact, but risk mitigation and safe working practices are paramount. If using doubles, stage shots to preserve the illusion and comic timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy, schedule discipline, and budget adherence
rubrics_metrics.description: Keaton's MGM film Parlor, Bedroom and Bath was commercially successful and notable for coming in under budget and ahead of schedule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Efficient production management can coincide with better outcomes; aim for tight scheduling and budget discipline without compromising essential rehearsal and staging needed for complex physical gags.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of visual tone and audience cues
rubrics_metrics.description: Keaton used intertitles and mock-serious opening intertitles (e.g., The Frozen North) to set a parody tone and ensure audiences picked up on the comic intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear visual or textual cues so the audience understands whether a piece is parody, sincere drama, or farce. In silent/visual comedy, intertitles, costume, and staging can set expectations and prevent misreading of tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Staging gags over heavy dialogue or verbal explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Keaton favored staging gags and long pantomime sequences rather than relying on scripted dialogue; this was partly why some of his MGM talkies felt compromised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In visual comedy prioritize staged sight-gags and physical beats over expository dialogue; when transitioning formats (silent→sound), find ways to preserve visual joke emphasis rather than substituting talk for action.
